These risks are demonstrate why large companies such as General Atomics are well suited for short-term projects with rapid ramp up periods. They have the critical mass of employees needed for rapid reassignment to make a project successful, as well as the cashflow and facilities that can be rapidly repurposed, and they have the lineage of know how required to complete these complex engineering projects. Even with these immense resources, a large company such as General Atomics are reluctant to take on the risk of these capital and personnel investments, as failures of prior large scale projects such as the Superconducting Super Collider demonstrate macro-economics as well as politics can end even the largest projects. With equipment such as electron beam welding, there is a potential to reduce risk by serving multiple industries. This may not be possible if there are concerns of cross contamination between materials. The clean room and electron beam welding facilities may be able to support normal conducting, superconducting, and medical applications. Welding could also be performed for nuclear components, pressure vessels, and other scientific devices including waveguides, gyrotron components, and klystron components. Zanon is an example of an Italian company that started as and maintains a major pressure vessel division but has successfully transitioned that capability to SRF niobium cavity production. Conversely, Babcock and Wilcox is a US pressure vessel manufacturer best known for their nuclear reactor fabrication capabilities that attempted to enter the SRF cavity production market but lost out on large contracts to European competitors during the 1980s.[66] However, the success of the SRF venture depended on international funding from countries across the world. Without even the DOE guaranteeing funding for a domestic accelerator facility, there would be little to no chance that a facility could operate let alone compete with international manufacturers. Access to Electron Beam Welding Job Shop and Potential Alternatives: When comparing potential job shop partners, OEMs primarily want to sell, maintain and upgrade equipment. On the other hand, job shops are seeking maximize welding time via long term contracts spread across many industries and customers. The DOE scientific lab requirements often do not fit within these constraints. DOE accelerator labs have been having increasing difficulty having job shops complete their work in a timely manner or at all. This is not limited to accelerator science, the DOE High Flux Isotope Reactor (HFIR) at ORNL requires repair and maintenance, and managers are unable to get any EBW job shop to accept the work associated with making high mix/low volume components. Engineers are examining a redesign of certain HFIR sub-systems to TIG weld instead of electron beam weld as was previously done. This redesign will require major engineering and quality work.
